Pence
PENS
n. (plural of penny)
Plural of penny; the KJV renders the Greek dēnarion (denarius) as penny, with pence as the plural. The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin, approximately one day’s wage for an ordinary laborer in the first-century Mediterranean world.

📖 Biblical Definition

Pence is the plural of penny—the KJV’s rendering of the Greek dēnarion (denarius), the standard Roman silver coin worth approximately one day’s wage for an ordinary laborer. The denarius was the most commonly-used larger denomination in first-century Palestine, the coin of ordinary commerce and standard payments. Several structural biblical moments turn on the denarius. First, the parable of the laborers in the vineyard (Matt 20:1-16). The householder agrees with the laborers hired at dawn for a penny a day (a fair daily wage); throughout the day he hires additional workers; at the day’s end he pays each one a penny, beginning with those hired last. The first-hired murmur that they received the same as those who worked only one hour; the householder responds that he has done them no wrong (a penny is a fair daily wage and what was agreed), that he is free to do with his own what he will, that the last shall be first and the first last. The parable teaches the sovereignty of God in dispensing reward, the equality of access to the kingdom, and the impropriety of comparing one’s portion with another’s. Second, the question about tribute to Caesar (Matt 22:15-22; Mark 12:13-17). The Pharisees and Herodians try to entangle Christ: is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not? Christ asks for the tribute money and is brought a penny (denarius); He asks whose image and superscription are on it; they answer, Caesar’s; He concludes, render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. The penny becomes the visual aid for one of the most important political-theological teachings of the New Testament: civil obligation to the magistrate within the larger total obligation to God. Third, the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30-37). The Samaritan, having bound up the wounded man, brought him to the inn, and taken care of him, on the next day gave the host two pence (two denarii) with the instruction to take care of the wounded man and the promise that whatsoever the host spent more, the Samaritan would repay at his return. The two pence—two days’ wages—is a substantial advance for ongoing care, illustrating the costly practical love the parable models. Fourth, the parable of the unmerciful servant’s fellow-servant (Matt 18:28): the forgiven servant grabs his fellow-servant by the throat for a debt of an hundred pence—a substantial sum (100 days’ wages) but trivial compared to his own forgiven debt of 10,000 talents. The pence-amount in the parable is the proportionate small-debt against the forgiven larger-debt, illustrating the ingratitude of refusing to forgive minor offenses after receiving massive forgiveness.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 treats PENCE as the plural of penny; in scripture, the KJV renders the Greek denarius as penny, the standard Roman silver coin worth one day’s wage for an ordinary laborer; significant in the Parable of the Laborers (Matt 20), the Tribute-to-Caesar (Matt 22:21), the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:35), and the Unmerciful Servant (Matt 18:28).

expand to see more

PENCE, n. plural — The plural of penny; in scripture, the KJV plural of the Greek denarius (e.g., Matt 18:28, an hundred pence; Luke 10:35, two pence).

DENARIUS, n. — A Roman silver coin of the early empire, equal to about 16 cents in silver, or the day’s wage of a laborer in the first-century Mediterranean world.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 20:2 — "And when he had agreed with the labourers for a penny a day, he sent them into his vineyard."

Matthew 22:19-21 — "Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny. And he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription? They say unto him, Caesar’s. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s."

Luke 10:35 — "And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee."

Matthew 18:28 — "But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The pence-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the modern translation drift that has often substituted vague day’s wage or specific denarius for the KJV’s penny, losing the precision the KJV preserves—and by the consequent loss of pastoral attention to the precise sums Christ’s parables use (one penny, two pence, hundred pence) as carriers of theological substance.

expand to see more

Modern translations have variously rendered the Greek denarius as denarius (the technical name), day’s wage (the functional value), or silver coin (the general category). Each has its merits; each loses something the KJV’s penny preserves. The KJV-reader accustomed to the coin-vocabulary tracks the precise sums Christ’s parables use: one penny is the day’s wage of the vineyard laborer; two pence is the Samaritan’s advance to the innkeeper; an hundred pence is the small-debt against the unmerciful servant’s 10,000 talents; the penny shown to Christ in the tribute question is the standard Roman coin with Caesar’s image and superscription. The precise sums matter: the parable’s force often depends on the proportional contrast (two pence is substantial care; an hundred pence is meaningful but trivial against 10,000 talents) that the modern flattening can muddy.

The deeper pastoral substance is that Christ’s parables use the precise small-and-mid-sized sums of everyday life as the carriers of teaching about justice, generosity, forgiveness, and the kingdom’s economics. The vineyard penny teaches God’s sovereign generosity in dispensing reward; the tribute penny teaches the proper rendering of civil obligation within total obligation to God; the Samaritan’s two pence teaches costly practical love; the unmerciful servant’s hundred pence teaches the obligation of the forgiven-much to forgive the small. The recovery of the coin-vocabulary is therefore not antiquarianism but the recovery of a register of teaching that runs through the Gospels with concrete pastoral substance. Christ teaches in the currency of His hearers; the contemporary reader who learns the coin-precision hears the parables in the register Christ used.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dēnarion (denarius), KJV penny (plural pence); the standard Roman silver coin worth one day’s wage; significant in the Parable of the Laborers (Matt 20), the Tribute-to-Caesar (Matt 22:19-21), the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:35), and the Unmerciful Servant (Matt 18:28).

expand to see more

Greek dēnarion (G1220) — denarius (16 NT uses).

Latin denarius — literally tenner, originally worth ten asses; the standard Roman silver coin.

Greek misthos (G3408) — wages (the day’s pay; cousin term to the denarius as day’s wage).

Hebrew shekel (H8255) — shekel (the OT cousin standard, larger than the denarius).
